title: Quick Sampler Tricks
intro: Quick Sampler turns any sound into a playable instrument in about three seconds. It is the fastest route from “that noise is interesting” to “that noise is now a bassline”.

tips.t: Drag any audio onto an empty track area while holding nothing
tips.d: Logic offers to create a Quick Sampler instrument from it. You can drag from the Finder, the browser, or straight from another region in your project.

tips.t: Know the four modes and pick deliberately
tips.d: Classic for straight playback, One Shot for drums and stabs, Slice to chop a loop across the keyboard, Recorder to sample live input. Choosing the mode is 90% of the work.

tips.t: Use Slice mode with Transient detection on any break
tips.d: Load a drum loop, switch to Slice, and every hit is mapped to its own key. Hit “Create MIDI” or drag the MIDI out and you have the original groove, fully rearrangeable.

tips.t: Change slice division to Beat or Division instead of Transient
tips.d: For loops with soft transients, slicing at a fixed 1/8 or 1/16 gives cleaner results than transient detection.

tips.t: Sample directly from your input with Recorder mode
tips.d: Quick Sampler will record from a mic or a bus. Sample your own reverb tail, your own voice, or another track in the project.

tips.t: Drag audio directly from the Tracks area into a loaded Quick Sampler
tips.d: Replaces the sample while keeping every setting — your filter, envelope and effects stay exactly as dialled in.

tips.t: Use Flex/Follow Tempo to lock a loop to the project
tips.d: Turn on Flex in Quick Sampler and the sample follows tempo changes without changing pitch.

tips.t: Set the root key correctly or nothing will be in tune
tips.d: Quick Sampler guesses the pitch. If your bass is a semitone out across the keyboard, this is why. Set it manually in the Pitch section.

tips.t: Turn on Loop with crossfade for infinite sustain
tips.d: Set the loop start and end in the sustain portion of the sample and add a crossfade. A one‑second sample becomes a pad you can hold forever.

tips.t: Use the Sample Start modulation for variation
tips.d: Modulate sample start with velocity or randomness and each hit sounds slightly different, which stops sampled drums sounding machine‑gunned.

tips.t: Reverse the sample for instant risers
tips.d: One button in the waveform display. Reverse a crash, put it before the drop, done.

tips.t: Use the Filter and its envelope, not an insert plugin
tips.d: The internal filter is per‑voice, so it responds to every note independently. An insert filter processes the summed output and sounds completely different.

tips.t: Drag MIDI out of Slice mode into the Tracks area
tips.d: The generated MIDI plays the slices in the original order. Now shuffle the notes and the break rearranges itself.

tips.t: Convert Quick Sampler to Sampler for full control
tips.d: Swap the instrument slot from Quick Sampler to Sampler and your loaded content transfers across automatically. Do it when you need multiple velocity layers, round robins or key zones. It is a one-way trip — Sampler settings will not open back up in Quick Sampler.

tips.t: Save your instrument as a patch immediately
tips.d: Chopped a break you like? Save it to the Library before you close the project, or it exists only in that one session.

tips.t: Use one Quick Sampler per element rather than one big kit
tips.d: Separate instances mean separate channel strips, separate processing and separate automation. Disk space is free; flexibility is not.
